title: Reductive Affine Invariant Theory and Geometric Quotients

items.title: Reductive and linearly reductive complex algebraic groups
items.statement: Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). A closed subgroup $U\subseteq G$ is **unipotent** if every non-zero finite-dimensional rational $U$-module has a non-zero $U$-fixed vector; this fixed-vector condition is the characterization used in Brion's Example 1.22 (equivalently, by the Lie-Kolchin theorem, $U$ is unipotent in the standard sense that it admits no non-trivial rational characters and all its elements are unipotent). The group $G$ is **reductive** if it has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup, and **linearly reductive** if every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely reducible, i.e. a direct sum of simple $G$-submodules ([[def-completely-reducible-representation]], [[def-semisimple-module]]). Over $\mathbf C$ the two notions coincide, by the unitary trick: every complex reductive affine algebraic group is linearly reductive, and conversely a linearly reductive $G$ has no non-trivial closed normal unipotent subgroup ([[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]]). Both notions depend only on the identity component in the sense that $G$ is reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is. The equivalence is false in characteristic $p>0$ and must never be extended: $\mathrm{SL}_2$ in characteristic $2$ has non-semisimple representations, and a linear algebraic group over a field of characteristic $p\neq0$ is linearly reductive if and only if its identity component is of multiplicative type and $p$ does not divide the component index (Milne Remark 12.56).
items.strategy: Definition record following Brion Definitions 1.20-1.21, Example 1.22 and Theorem 1.23 (iii)-(iv), printed pp. 7-8, with the positive-characteristic boundary from Milne Definition 12.52, Example 12.55 and Remark 12.56, printed pp. 248-249. The equivalence over $\mathbf C$ is announced here and proved in [[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]]. No claim of equivalence in positive characteristic; no notion of geometric reductivity is introduced.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Groups (corrected 2022 printing, Cambridge University Press)

items.title: Complex affine algebraic groups are smooth
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then every point of $G$ is a regular point of the affine algebraic set $G$; equivalently $G$ is smooth over $\mathbf C$, and its local rings are regular local rings. In particular $G$ is a smooth variety of pure dimension $\dim G$ ([[def-dimension-classical-variety]]).
items.strategy: The group $G$ is non-empty, hence its regular locus is a non-empty dense open subset ([[thm-nonempty-regular-locus-reduced-variety-perfect-field]]). For $g\in G$, left translation by $g$ is an isomorphism of affine algebraic sets (multiplication and inversion are morphisms in [[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]), so it carries the non-empty regular locus onto a non-empty open subset; every point lies in some translate of the regular locus. Hence $G$ is regular everywhere, and regular equals smooth over the perfect field $\mathbf C$ ([[thm-regular-equals-smooth-over-perfect-field]]). This is Brion Lemma 1.3 (printed p. 3).

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: Categorical and geometric quotients of classical varieties
items.statement: Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group acting algebraically on a classical variety $X$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]], [[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). A $G$-invariant morphism $\pi:X\to Y$ is a **categorical quotient** if every $G$-invariant morphism $f:X\to Z$ of classical varieties factors uniquely as $f=\varphi\circ\pi$ with $\varphi:Y\to Z$ a morphism. It is a **geometric quotient** (Brion Definition 1.18) if (i) $\pi$ is surjective and its fibres are exactly the $G$-orbits, (ii) a subset $U\subseteq Y$ is open if and only if $\pi^{-1}(U)$ is open in $X$, and (iii) for every open $U\subseteq Y$ the pullback of regular functions is an isomorphism $\mathcal O_Y(U)\to \mathcal O_X(\pi^{-1}(U))^G$ onto the $G$-invariant regular functions on the preimage. A geometric quotient is a categorical quotient and is unique up to unique isomorphism; when it exists its underlying topological space is the orbit space $X/G$ with the quotient topology. For an affine $G$-variety $X$ whose invariant algebra $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is finitely generated, the affine model is the morphism $\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ of an affine $G$-variety; for a reductive $G$, the theorem below proves finite generation and makes this a categorical quotient with one closed orbit in each fibre.
items.strategy: Definition record following Brion Definition 1.18 and the paragraph after Theorem 1.24 (printed pp. 7-9). The scheme-theoretic fppf notion of a quotient sheaf on the AG-ACT-1 page is a different object and is not identified with this classical notion here. The final sentence records the affine model used later, without asserting finite generation here. To justify the general geometric-quotient implication, an invariant morphism h:X -> Z is constant on orbit fibres, defining a set map hbar:Y -> Z. Quotient topology makes hbar continuous: inverse images are open exactly when their pullbacks along pi are open, and h is continuous. On every target affine chart V, each coordinate function pulls back to an invariant regular function on pi^{-1}(hbar^{-1}(V)); property (iii) descends it uniquely to a regular function on hbar^{-1}(V). The local affine morphism criterion then makes hbar regular. Surjectivity ensures uniqueness. This proves categorical universality for all classical varieties directly from the definition, without the affine-target limitation. The final affine model sentence refers specifically to the commissioned reductive affine theorem; arbitrary nonreductive actions are not certified by finite generation and orbit counts alone. In the classical register, Spec of a finitely generated reduced complex algebra denotes its associated affine variety of complex closed points with the classical regular-function sheaf; no identification with the space of every scheme prime is used. For empty X its coordinate algebra is zero and its quotient and stable locus are empty; finite generation and universal properties are immediate and fibre assertions are vacuous. The maximal-ideal argument concerns nonempty X. Step7 repair: the affine model explicitly requires finite generation; the reductive theorem proves that hypothesis. The general geometric-to-categorical argument is unchanged.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: Orbit dimension and closed orbits for complex group actions
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the orbit and dimension suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group acting algebraically on a classical variety $X$ ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]), and let $x\in X$. Then: (a) $G_x$ and $(G^\circ)_x$ have the same dimension, the orbit $Gx$ is a finite union of $G^\circ$-orbits of common dimension $\dim G^\circ-\dim G_x$, and $\dim G=\dim G_x+\dim Gx$; (b) every irreducible component of the orbit closure $\overline{Gx}$ has dimension $\dim Gx$, and $\overline{Gx}$ is the union of $Gx$ and of orbits of strictly smaller dimension; (c) every orbit of minimal dimension in $X$ is closed, and every orbit closure contains a closed orbit. Assertion (c) is the input used later for the unique closed orbit in a quotient fibre.
items.strategy: Locally derive the identity component as a normal irreducible clopen subgroup with finitely many component cosets from group smoothness, the unique component at a regular point, and the finite-component theorem. Apply this also to the reduced classical stabilizer to prove dim (G^circ)_x=dim G_x. The connected orbit suppliers give dimension and boundary formulas. Distinct connected-group orbits cannot meet the other equal-dimensional closures, since equal closures would give intersecting dense open orbits. Their finite closed union gives the full orbit dimension and equidimensional closure. Every boundary orbit has smaller dimension; choosing least dimension in a closure gives a closed orbit. AC is inherited from the named suppliers. This is Brion Lemma 1.3 and Proposition 1.11, printed pp. 3-4; scheme stabilizer fibres are left cosets, with dimensions unchanged by reduction.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: Stable points of an affine action
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group acting algebraically on an affine algebraic set $X$ ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). A point $x\in X$ is **stable** if (i) its orbit $Gx$ is closed in $X$ and (ii) its stabilizer $G_x$ is finite, equivalently $\dim G_x=0$ ([[lem-orbit-dimension-and-closed-orbits-for-complex-group-actions]], [[def-dimension-classical-variety]]); here $G_x$ is a closed subgroup of the finite-type group $G$. The **stable locus** $X^s\subseteq X$ is the set of stable points, and the **unstable locus** is its complement. Stability implies that the orbit is closed; the converse fails: the trivial action of $\mathbf G_m$ on a point has closed orbit but positive-dimensional stabilizer. Stability is preserved by replacing $G$ with $G^\circ$.
items.strategy: Definition record following Brion Definition 1.25 (printed p. 9), with the finite stabilizer condition expressed by dimension using the closedness of the stabilizer and finite type over $\mathbf C$; the final strictness remark is Brion Example 1.27(1) (quotient of a point) and is made explicit as a counterexample on the companion page.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: Complete reducibility and the Reynolds operator for a complex reductive group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex reductive affine algebraic group ([[def-reductive-and-linearly-reductive-over-c]]). (i) Every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely reducible, so $G$ is linearly reductive. (ii) Every rational $G$-module $V$ is a direct sum of simple submodules; the invariant subspace $V^G$ therefore has a unique $G$-stable complement $V_G$, the sum of all simple submodules on which $G$ acts non-trivially. The projection $R_V:V\to V^G$ with kernel $V_G$ is the **Reynolds operator** of $V$; it is $G$-equivariant, restricts to the identity of $V^G$, and is natural: for every morphism $f:V\to W$ of rational $G$-modules one has $R_W\circ f=f^G\circ R_V$, and if $f$ is surjective then so is $f^G:V^G\to W^G$. (iii) If $A$ is a commutative $G$-algebra on which $G$ acts by algebra automorphisms and which is a rational $G$-module, then $R_A$ is $A^G$-linear: $R_A(ab)=a\,R_A(b)$ for $a\in A^G$, $b\in A$. (iv) When $K\subseteq G$ is a compact subgroup whose Zariski closure in $G$ is all of $G$, the Reynolds operator of a finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is the invariant average $R_V(v)=\int_K g\cdot v\,dg$ with respect to normalized Haar measure; in particular $R_V(v)$ is the unique element of $V^G$ in the convex hull of the $K$-orbit of $v$.
items.strategy:
Algebraic bridge, independently reconstructed below; Milne Algebraic Groups22.41-22.43 is a full second treatment of the conclusion, and Milne Lie Algebras3.7 and5.20 provides the proved local Lie inputs. Brion1.23(iii)->(iv) is the compact-density implication only: its omitted (ii)->(iii) compact-existence direction is not invoked. Clause(iv) of this item is conditional on the supplied K, so proving existence of K is not needed for the commissioned claim. The faithful closed embedding is [[lem-affine-algebraic-group-faithful-rational-representation]]. G's coordinate Hopf identities and the rational-module/finite-coefficient conventions are [[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]. All complex group reductions used below are smooth by [[lem-complex-algebraic-groups-are-smooth]], and connected smooth algebraic groups are integral by [[lem-nonaffine-connected-group-geometrically-connected]]. Closed matrix subgroups are Lie groups by [[thm-cartans-closed-subgroup-theorem]]; use [[prop-exponential-map-is-natural-for-lie-group-homomorphisms]] and [[thm-one-parameter-subgroups-are-exactly-exponentials]] to identify their exponentials with the ordinary matrix series: that series is a one-parameter subgroup with the prescribed initial derivative, so uniqueness applies. At the identity [[thm-ag-perfect-field-jacobian-regularity]] supplies local polynomial equations with independent complex Jacobian, and [[thm-holomorphic-implicit-function-theorem]] makes their zero locus a complex manifold with tangent the same Jacobian kernel as the algebraic tangent. Empty equation blocks give ambient open charts; zero-dimensional charts give isolated points. Multiplication and inversion are holomorphic in these charts, so the underlying real manifold is a matrix Lie group of twice the complex dimension; the differential representation is a Lie representation by [[thm-differential-of-a-lie-group-homomorphism-is-a-lie-algebra-homomorphism]]. For clarity the full local bridge follows; every use of a local Lie input is stated with its actual hypotheses. Let G be connected reductive complex affine algebraic group, embedded faithfully and closed in GL(W). Write g for its complex tangent Lie algebra, and r for its Lie radical. G is smooth (local batch16 lemma), integral (published lem-nonaffine-connected-group-geometrically-connected), and a closed matrix Lie group. Complex algebraic smoothness identifies its algebraic tangent with its matrix Lie algebra; exp(tX) belongs to G for X in g and complex t. A Lie-invariant subspace of any rational module is G-invariant: its stabilizer is a closed algebraic subgroup, its Lie algebra contains g, and smoothness plus equal dimensions force the stabilizer to contain the identity component G. This also upgrades Lie-invariant flags. These facts use the published closed subgroup and exponential interfaces and ordinary Jacobian charts; no analytic connectedness theorem is needed.

1. [[cor-simultaneous-upper-triangularization-of-solvable-lie-algebra-representations]] supplies a basis in which r acts upper triangular on W; let lambda_1,...,lambda_N be its diagonal linear forms. The radical is characteristic ([[prop-the-radical-is-characteristic-and-the-radical-quotient-has-zero-radical]]), so Ad(G) preserves r. Conjugation gives equivalent r-representations. More explicitly the characteristic polynomial of A in r is product(T-lambda_i(A)); for every A in r each transformed diagonal value equals one of lambda_j(A). A linear functional not equal to any lambda_j can be distinguished from all of them by choosing A outside finitely many proper hyperplanes. Thus Ad(h) permutes the finite set of diagonal linear forms, without any assertion that the triangular flag itself is G-stable. Each algebraic map h -> lambda_i circ Ad(h) has connected image in a finite subset of r*, hence is constant. Differentiating at identity gives lambda_i([X,A])=0 for X in g and A in r. Thus n=[g,r] is an Ad(G)-stable Lie ideal of g represented by strictly upper triangular matrices.

2. Let N be the subgroup generated by exp(n); each exp(tA) is polynomial in t because A is strictly upper triangular. Its Zariski closure U is a closed subgroup of G, contained in the upper unitriangular group and normal because Ad(G)n=n and conjugation commutes with exponentials. U is connected because N is generated by connected algebraic curves through identity and closure preserves connectedness. To check the definition's fixed-vector characterization of unipotence rather than merely assert it from its matrix realization, Lie(U) is solvable and every finite-dimensional rational U-representation has a Lie-invariant flag by Lie triangularization, hence a U-invariant flag by the stabilizer/dimension argument. Every diagonal character is trivial on exp(tA): its restriction is an algebraic homomorphism A1_add -> Gm, whose coordinate polynomial and inverse are both polynomial, hence constant. It is therefore trivial on dense N and on U. The full flag is consequently unitriangular, so its first line is fixed. U is unipotent in the exact definition and reductivity gives U=1, forcing n=0. Since every centre lies in the radical, r=z(g). [[thm-levi-decomposition]] gives g=z direct sum s with s semisimple.

3. For X in z, exp(tX) is central in G by the closed-stabilizer/dimension argument. Use [[thm-additive-jordan-chevalley-decomposition]] over the perfect field C to write X=Xs+Xn as its commuting ordinary matrix Jordan parts; this splitting is in End(W), without assuming either part lies in g. For any regular function P on GL(W) vanishing on exp(tX), substituting the exponential gives a finite sum sum_mu p_mu(t)exp(mu t), where each p_mu is a polynomial; determinant denominators only add exponential factors. Distinct exponential functions exp(mu t) are linearly independent over C[t]: if such a finite relation exists, choose a term mu0 and apply product_mu!=mu0 (D-mu)^(1+deg p_mu), killing all others; on the mu0 term each D+(mu0-mu) is invertible on polynomials of bounded degree, so the result is a nonzero polynomial times exp(mu0 t), contradiction. Hence every p_mu vanishes identically. Substituting exp(tXs)exp(uXn) now gives sum_mu p_mu(u)exp(mu t)=0 for independently chosen t,u, since only Xn contributes polynomial coefficients. Therefore every such P vanishes on exp(uXn), so that subgroup is contained in the Zariski closure of exp(tX), which is central in G. If Xn is nonzero its one-parameter polynomial image is isomorphic to Ga: choose an entry of log(1+M) (the finite polynomial logarithm on unipotent matrices) to recover u. This is a closed image since log identifies it with the closed line C Xn; exp and log are inverse finite polynomials on nilpotent/unipotent matrices. Ga's rational representations have a fixed vector by the flag argument of step2, so it is a nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup of G, contradiction. Thus Xn=0. Every X in z is semisimple as a matrix.

4. [[thm-simultaneous-diagonalisation-of-commuting-diagonalisable-endomorphisms]] applies to the commuting family z in End(W). The Zariski closure T of the subgroup generated by exp(z) is consequently contained in the diagonal torus, central in G, and its Lie algebra contains z. It need not be identified abstractly with a torus or placed in a central isogeny. Its coordinate ring is a quotient of C[t1^{+-1},...,tN^{+-1}], and is linearly spanned by the restrictions of monomial characters. Distinct characters of any group are linearly independent: a shortest nontrivial relation, evaluated at hg and subtracting one character(h) times the relation at g, yields a shorter relation unless all characters agree. This proves independence and shows the distinct restricted characters form a basis of C[T]. For a finite-dimensional rational T-module, expand the coaction of v in that basis; coassociativity with Delta chi=chi tensor chi makes the coefficients chi-weight vectors, and the counit makes their sum v. Thus every rational G-module of finite dimension decomposes into T-character spaces, which are G-stable because T is central; its G-submodule W0 decomposes into the intersections with those same spaces. The Lie algebra z acts scalarly on each character space since z is contained in Lie(T). [[thm-weyls-complete-reducibility-theorem]] splits the semisimple Lie algebra s on each character space, supplying an s-stable complement of W0 intersect that space. Scalar z action makes those complements g-stable, and the closed-stabilizer/dimension argument makes their direct sum G-stable. This proves complete reducibility for connected G.

5. For possibly disconnected reductive G, first G^circ is reductive: any nontrivial closed normal unipotent subgroup U0 of G^circ has finitely many conjugates Ui under G. Their product is a normal subgroup of G and is unipotent. To substantiate the product assertion using the exact fixed-vector definition, for a rational module V each V^Ui is nonzero and stable under every Uj because each Ui is normal in G^circ. Restrict successively and obtain a common fixed vector; repeat on successive quotients for a full common invariant flag. Thus all Ui are simultaneously unitriangular in a faithful module; the closure of their generated subgroup is normal in G and unipotent by the same flag/character reasoning. Reductivity forces U0=1. Apply step4 to G^circ. If W0 is G-stable choose a G^circ-equivariant projection p onto W0 and average hph^{-1} over one representative of each of the finitely many G/G^circ components; normality makes the resulting projection independent of representatives, G-equivariant and identity on W0. Its kernel is the desired complement.


6. For (ii), every vector of a rational module lies in a finite-dimensional G-submodule by its definition; part(i) decomposes that submodule as a finite sum of simples, so the whole module is a sum of simple submodules. Under AC, [[thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-semisimple-modules]] makes this an algebraic direct sum. Let V_G be the sum of all nontrivial simple submodules. No nontrivial simple module maps nontrivially to a trivial module: its nonzero image would be simple and its kernel zero, making it trivial. Thus the canonical trivial-isotypic part V^G and V_G are complementary; any G-stable complement to V^G has no trivial simple submodule and equals V_G. Equivariant maps preserve these two types, proving naturality of the projection R. If f is surjective, lift w in W^G to v and obtain w=R_W(fv)=f(R_Vv), proving surjectivity on invariants. Multiplication by a in A^G is equivariant, so naturality proves R_A(ab)=aR_A(b). The declared AC is inherited from the sum-of-simples supplier and the geometric/Lie suppliers; finite component averaging itself makes only finite choices.
7. For (iv), view the given compact K as a compact Lie subgroup of the closed matrix group using Cartan's theorem. Continuous finite-dimensional orbit maps are integrable for its normalized Haar measure, supplied by [[cor-normalized-haar-measure-on-a-compact-lie-group]]. Translation invariance ([[prop-integration-against-haar-is-invariant-under-translations-and-conjugation]]) makes the average K-fixed; the stabilizer of the averaged vector is Zariski closed and contains dense K, so the average is G-fixed. The average fixes V^G and preserves V_G, hence vanishes on V_G and equals R_V. To prove the exact convex-hull assertion, in the underlying real dimension d every finite convex combination can be reduced to at most d+1 orbit vectors: if more occur their augmented vectors (v,1) are linearly dependent, and subtracting an appropriate multiple of that dependence from the weights retains nonnegativity and their sum while making one weight zero. Repeat finitely. Therefore the convex hull of the compact K-orbit is the image of its (d+1)-fold product times the compact coefficient simplex, and is compact and closed. Uniform continuity of the orbit map on compact K gives finite measurable partitions and convex finite sums converging to its Haar average (choose one value per cell, weighted by the cell's measure); closedness puts R_V(v) in the convex hull. Since R_V(gv)=R_V(v), linearity implies R_V equals the constant R_V(v) on every point of that hull; an invariant point w is fixed by R_V, hence w=R_V(v). This proves uniqueness. Compact subgroup existence is not asserted by this conditional clause.
8. The converse announced in the definition is proved without the missing compact-existence theorem: if every finite-dimensional rational G-module is semisimple and U is a closed normal unipotent subgroup, each simple module S has nonzero S^U by the stated definition of unipotence; normality makes S^U G-stable and simplicity gives S^U=S. A faithful finite-dimensional module is thus fixed by U, forcing U=1. The equivalence of reductivity for G and G^circ is the finite-conjugate argument of step5. Positive characteristic is outside every Lie argument here. For the finite-component reduction, smoothness makes the irreducible components disjoint (their local regular rings are domains), so they are open and closed and are also connected components. Translation permutes them. The identity component is closed and normal: multiplication and inversion preserve it by connectedness, and conjugation fixes the identity. Its cosets are the components, and there are finitely many because the affine variety is Noetherian. Thus the averaging index is finite, without assuming analytic connectedness.

items.title: A positively graded Noetherian algebra is finitely generated over its degree-zero part
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $A=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}A_n$ be a graded commutative ring with $A_0$ a field, and suppose $A$ is Noetherian ([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]], [[def-noetherian-ring]]). Then $A$ is a finitely generated $A_0$-algebra ([[def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras]]).
items.strategy: The ideal $A_+=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}A_n$ is finitely generated because $A$ is Noetherian ([[thm-noetherian-ring-ideal-characterisations]]); since $A_+$ is a homogeneous ideal, it has homogeneous generators $g_1,\dots,g_m$ of positive degrees ([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]). One proves by induction on the degree that every homogeneous $f\in A$ lies in $A_0[g_1,\dots,g_m]$: for $\deg f>0$ write $f=\sum r_ig_i$ with $\deg r_i=\deg f-\deg g_i<\deg f$ (possible by homogeneity of the graded pieces), and apply the induction hypothesis to the $r_i$. Hence $A=A_0[g_1,\dots,g_m]$. This is the graded Nakayama argument used by Brion in the proof of Theorem 1.24(i) (printed p. 9) and by Popov-Vinberg in the proof of Theorem 3.6 (printed pp. 186-187).

items.title: The Reynolds operator and the ideal theory of the invariant subring
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]); write $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $R_X:A\to A^G$ be the Reynolds operator of [[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]]. Then: (a) $R_X$ is $A^G$-linear, idempotent, and its image is exactly $A^G$; (b) for every ideal $I\subseteq A^G$ one has $R_X(IA)=I$, and consequently the map $I\mapsto IA$ is injective on ideals of $A^G$ and $A^G$ is Noetherian whenever $A$ is Noetherian; (c) if $\varphi:A\to B$ is a surjective $G$-equivariant homomorphism of rational $G$-algebras, then $\varphi(A^G)=B^G$; (d) if $A$ carries a $G$-stable grading and an ideal is homogeneous, the same conclusions hold in the graded subalgebra of invariants.
items.strategy: Part (a) is (iii) of the bridge theorem plus the identity $R_X|A^G=\mathrm{id}$. Part (b) is Brion's step in the proof of Theorem 1.24(i) (printed p. 9): $IA$ is $G$-stable, so $R_X(IA)=IR_X(A)=IA^G=I$; an ascending chain of ideals of $A^G$ gives an ascending chain of ideals of the Noetherian ring $A$ ([[def-noetherian-ring]]), which stabilizes, and applying $R_X$ back gives stabilization. Part (c) is the naturality property (ii) of the bridge theorem: $\varphi(R_X a)=R_B(\varphi a)$ and $\varphi$ is surjective. Part (d) follows because the projections onto the G-stable graded pieces are equivariant; naturality makes R preserve each degree, and homogeneous ideals remain homogeneous under R. The same ideal-extension and surjective graded-map arguments then apply. This isolates the three computations used repeatedly in Theorem 1.24 and Proposition 1.26.

items.title: Invariants of a finite-dimensional module are finitely generated
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional rational module over a complex reductive affine algebraic group $G$ ([[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]]). Then $\mathbb C[V]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra.
items.strategy: The polynomial ring $A=\mathbb C[V]$ carries the positive grading $A=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}A_n$ by total degree with $A_0=\mathbb C$ and each $A_n$ finite-dimensional; the action of $G$ preserves the grading (the action is linear), so $A^G=\bigoplus_n A_n^G$ is a positively graded $\mathbb C$-algebra. The polynomial algebra is Noetherian by [[lem-finite-variable-polynomial-algebras-over-fields-are-noetherian-direct]]. By [[lem-reynolds-operator-and-invariant-subring-properties]](b) applied to $A$, the ring $A^G$ is Noetherian, and [[lem-positively-graded-noetherian-algebra-is-finitely-generated]] makes it finitely generated over $\mathbb C$. This is Brion's proof of Theorem 1.24(i) in the case $X=V$ (printed p. 9) and Popov-Vinberg Theorem 3.6.

items.title: Finite generation of invariants and the affine categorical quotient
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then: (i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring $\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism $\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient ([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism $Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable $Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of $\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.
items.strategy: Brion's proof of Theorem 1.24 (printed pp. 8-9) with the two reductions isolated above. Write $A=\mathbb C[X]$. (i) By [[lem-reynolds-operator-and-invariant-subring-properties]](b), $A^G$ is Noetherian; less directly, the equivariant embedding $X\hookrightarrow V$ of [[thm-affine-algebraic-action-embeds-equivariantly-in-finite-dimensional-module]] gives a surjective $G$-algebra map $\mathbb C[V]\to A$, hence a surjection $\mathbb C[V]^G\to A^G$ by [[lem-reynolds-operator-and-invariant-subring-properties]](c), so finite generation of $A^G$ follows from [[lem-invariant-ring-of-finite-dimensional-module-is-finitely-generated]]. (ii)-(iii) For a maximal ideal $I\subseteq A^G$ put $J=IA$; then $J\cap A^G=R_X(J)=I\neq A^G$, so $J$ lies in a maximal ideal $M$ of $A$ with $M\cap A^G=I$ ([[thm-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal-ideal]]), and the Nullstellensatz dictionary ([[thm-classical-affine-nullstellensatz-correspondence]], [[thm-classical-affine-morphisms-coordinate-ring-antiequivalence]]) upgrades this to surjectivity of $X\to X/\!/G$, closedness and independence of generators. (iv) A surjection $A\to A/I$ of $G$-algebras induces a surjection of invariants by (c), ; use the ideal calculation detailed below, retaining radicals for reduced intersections. (v) Distinct closed orbits are separated by (iv); existence in every fibre is [[lem-orbit-dimension-and-closed-orbits-for-complex-group-actions]](c), since $\pi$ is constant on orbit closures. (vi) $X$ irreducible makes $A^G$ a domain with fraction field inside the fraction field of $A$, and normality passes because $A^G$ is integrally closed in $\operatorname{Frac}(A)^G$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the embedding and Nullstellensatz suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The preceding affine coordinate-ring argument proves universality initially for affine targets, not yet all classical varieties. Supply the following descent argument to establish the commissioned full categorical assertion. First, R extends to invariant principal localizations and gives (A_f)^G=(A^G)_f: an invariant fraction a/f^n equals R_A(a)/f^n, by naturality of R under A -> A_f and A_f^G-linearity, and the localization map on A^G is injective into A_f (an invariant numerator killed by a power of f is killed already in A^G). Thus the sheaf of invariants equals the structure sheaf of the quotient on its principal-open basis and on all opens by gluing. For a G-invariant morphism h:X -> Z to any separated classical variety, h is constant on each orbit closure, because the inverse image of its value (a closed point of Z) is closed; unique closed orbit per quotient fibre then makes h constant on that whole fibre. Write hbar for the induced set map on the quotient. Around hbar(q) choose affine open V in Z. The G-stable closed subset C=h^{-1}(Z\V) has closed image pi(C) by (iv), and q is outside that image, since its whole fibre maps into V. On an affine principal neighbourhood D(f) of q disjoint from pi(C), h maps X_f into V. Each coordinate of h|X_f is an invariant regular function, hence belongs to (A^G)_f by the proved localization identity. The coordinate-ring anti-equivalence yields a morphism D(f) -> V inducing hbar; these local morphisms agree by surjectivity of pi and the classical closed-point morphism criterion. They glue and prove existence; surjectivity proves uniqueness. For (iv), do not identify the reduced ideal of Y intersect Y' with I+J: it is sqrt(I+J). Prove the image equality on points instead. If q is in both images and m is its maximal ideal in A^G, the proper G-stable ideals I+mA and J+mA have invariant parts m; if their sum were A, Reynolds would imply 1 in m. Their sum is therefore proper and lies in a maximal ideal of A, whose closed point is in Y intersect Y' over q. Equivalently the same calculation with I+J+mA and R shows properness directly, because R(I),R(J) are contained in m. This proves the set-theoretic equality without a false radical identity. Normality uses integral closedness in Frac(A)^G: any element of Frac(A^G) integral over A^G is integral over A and hence lies in A, and invariance then places it in A^G. Normality of an irreducible affine classical variety is exactly normality of its local coordinate rings ([[def-normal-point-and-normal-variety]]); [[thm-normality-is-local-for-domains]] identifies that with integral closedness of the coordinate domain, in the convention of [[def-integral-closure-and-integrally-closed-domain]]. In the classical register, Spec of a finitely generated reduced complex algebra denotes its associated affine variety of complex closed points with the classical regular-function sheaf; no identification with the space of every scheme prime is used. For empty X its coordinate algebra is zero and its quotient and stable locus are empty; finite generation and universal properties are immediate and fibre assertions are vacuous. The maximal-ideal argument concerns nonempty X.

items.title: Semicontinuity of stabilizer and orbit dimension
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the local fibre-dimension supplier. Let $G$ be a complex affine algebraic group acting algebraically on a classical variety $X$ ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). For every integer $n$ the set $\{x\in X:\dim G_x\ge n\}$ is closed in $X$; equivalently $x\mapsto\dim G_x$ is upper semicontinuous and $x\mapsto\dim Gx$ is lower semicontinuous ([[def-dimension-classical-variety]]). In particular the set of points with infinite stabilizer is closed, and if $X$ is nonempty, the points with stabilizer of minimal dimension form a non-empty open subset.
items.strategy: Use the exact published general supplier [[lem-local-fibre-dimension-bound-via-polynomial-quasifiniteness]], clause 2, with its local-dimension convention [[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]]; this needs neither properness nor projectivity. Affine charts of a locally finite-type morphism give, for every source point a of fibre local dimension d, a source neighbourhood on which fibre local dimension is at most d. Therefore each locus of fibre local dimension at most n is open. Apply this to beta:G x X -> X x X, (g,x) -> (x,gx), taking the schemes associated to the classical varieties. At a closed point (g,x), the scheme fibre is a translate of G_x by [[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]; switching the two target factors reconciles that supplier's (gx,x) convention. The dimension here is the maximum dimension of a component through the point, not the dimension of its local ring. Translation on the reduction of G_x carries any closed point to any other, hence all its components have the same dimension and its local dimension at every closed point equals dim G_x. This uses the regular-locus/translation argument of [[lem-complex-algebraic-groups-are-smooth]] for the reduced classical subgroup and does not assume a possibly nonreduced stabilizer scheme is smooth. Pull back the open source locus along the identity section x -> (e,x). Thus {x:dim G_x <= n} is open, proving the asserted closed loci. Conjugation preserves stabilizer dimension, so these sets are G-stable. The identity dim Gx = dim G - dim G_x from [[lem-orbit-dimension-and-closed-orbits-for-complex-group-actions]] reverses the semicontinuity direction. Infinite stabilizer is equivalent to positive dimension for a finite-type complex algebraic group. If X is nonempty, its stabilizer dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by dim G; let m be the attained minimum. Its locus is the nonempty open {dim G_x < m+1}. AC is precisely inherited from the published local bound and orbit suppliers. Brion Lemma 1.14 and Stacks Morphisms Lemma 29.29.4 (tag 02FZ), whose full PDF proof reduces to Algebra Lemma 10.125.6, corroborate this exact interface.

The Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.29.4 (tag 02FZ)

items.title: Invariants separate a stable point from a disjoint closed invariant subset
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex reductive affine algebraic group acting algebraically on an affine algebraic set $X$, with categorical quotient $\pi:X\to X/\!/G$ ([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]]). Let $Z\subseteq X$ be closed and $G$-stable, and let $x\in X$ with $\pi(x)\notin\pi(Z)$. Then there exists $f\in\mathbb C[X]^G$ with $f(x)\neq0$ and $f|_Z=0$.
items.strategy: By [[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]](iv), $\pi(Z)$ is closed in the affine variety $X/\!/G$; a point outside a closed subset of an affine algebraic set is separated from it by a regular function ([[thm-classical-affine-nullstellensatz-correspondence]] applied in the affine coordinate ring of $X/\!/G$), say $\bar f$ with $\bar f(\pi x)\neq0$ and $\bar f|_{\pi(Z)}=0$; then $f=\pi^*(\bar f)\in\mathbb C[X]^G$ works. This is the first step of Brion's proof of Proposition 1.26 (printed pp. 9-10).

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: The stable locus has a geometric quotient
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a complex reductive affine algebraic group acting algebraically on an affine algebraic set $X$, with categorical quotient $\pi:X\to X/\!/G$ ([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]]) and stable locus $X^s$ ([[def-stable-points-of-an-affine-action]]). Then $\pi(X^s)$ is open in $X/\!/G$, one has $X^s=\pi^{-1}(\pi(X^s))$ (so that $X^s$ is an open $G$-stable subset of $X$), and the restriction $\pi^s:X^s\to\pi(X^s)$ is a geometric quotient ([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]). In particular the fibres of $\pi^s$ are exactly the $G$-orbits, each orbit in $X^s$ is closed in $X$, and $\mathcal O_{\pi(X^s)}=(\pi^s_*\mathcal O_{X^s})^G$.
items.strategy:
Brion's proof of Proposition 1.26 (printed pp. 9-10). Let $Y=\{y\in X:\dim G_y\ge1\}$, which is closed and $G$-stable by [[lem-stabilizer-dimension-semicontinuity]]. Let $x\in X^s$, so $Gx$ is closed and disjoint from $Y$; since fibres of $\pi$ contain a unique closed orbit ([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]](v)) and $\pi$ is constant on closures, $\pi(x)
otin\pi(Y)$, so [[lem-separation-of-disjoint-closed-invariant-subsets-by-an-invariant]] yields $f\in A^G$ with $f(x)
eq0$ and $f|_Y=0$. Put $X_f=\{f
eq0\}$; then $X_f=\pi^{-1}\pi(X_f)$, every stabilizer on $X_f$ is finite, and $X_f\subseteq X^s$: if $Gy$ were not closed then the unique closed orbit in $\overline{Gy}$ would contain a point $z$ with $f(z)=f(y)
eq0$ and $\dim G_z>\dim G_y=0$ by [[lem-orbit-dimension-and-closed-orbits-for-complex-group-actions]](b), a contradiction. Hence $\pi(X^s)$ is the union of the open sets $(X/\!/G)_f$ and is open. If $y\in\pi^{-1}\pi(x)$, then $Gx\subseteq\overline{Gy}$ and $Gy$ is closed, so $x\in Gy$ and $y\in Gx$; thus the fibres of $\pi^s$ are exactly the orbits, giving (i) of the geometric-quotient definition. Property (ii) is the complement-of-closed-image argument on the saturated stable locus detailed below, and (iii) is a sheaf-localization statement checked on the basis $(X/\!/G)_f$. This is Brion Proposition 1.26, printed pp. 9-10; see also Popov-Vinberg Section 4 and Dolgachev Chapter 6 for the quotient formulation. For the topological condition take an open W in X^s, also open in X since X^s is open; replace W by G.W, which has the same image and is open. Every fibre meeting X^s is a single orbit, so within pi(X^s) the image pi(W) is the complement of the closed image of X\G.W, using (iv). This proves the quotient topology without claiming that images of arbitrary G-stable opens outside the saturated stable locus are open. For the sheaf identity use (A_f)^G=(A^G)_f proved as part of the affine theorem, and glue over its principal-open basis. All AC assumptions of the quotient and orbit suppliers are carried throughout.

title: Reductive Affine Invariant Theory and Geometric Quotients — Examples

items.title: Invariants of the hyperbolic action of the multiplicative group on the plane
items.statement: Let $\mathbf G_m=\mathbb C^\times$ act on $\mathbb C^2$ by $t\cdot(x,y)=(tx,t^{-1}y)$ ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then the invariant subring of $\mathbb C[x,y]$ ([[def-classical-affine-coordinate-ring]]) is $\mathbb C[x,y]^{\mathbf G_m}=\mathbb C[xy]$, a polynomial ring in one variable; explicitly, a polynomial $f=\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}x^ay^b$ is invariant if and only if $c_{ab}=0$ for every pair with $a\neq b$ ([[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]).
items.strategy: The action on functions is $(t\cdot f)(x,y)=f(t^{-1}x,ty)$, so $t\cdot(x^ay^b)=t^{b-a}x^ay^b$ and $f$ is invariant if and only if $\sum_{a,b}c_{ab}(t^{b-a}-1)x^ay^b=0$ for every $t\in\mathbf G_m$. Since monomials are linearly independent ([[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]) this forces $c_{ab}(t^{b-a}-1)=0$ for every $t$; for $a\neq b$ choose $t\in\mathbb C^\times$ that is not a $(b-a)$-th root of unity (finitely many excluded values, $\mathbb C^\times$ infinite), giving $c_{ab}=0$. Thus the invariants are the polynomials in $xy$, and the map $\mathbb C[z]\to\mathbb C[x,y]^{\mathbf G_m}$, $z\mapsto xy$, is injective because the monomials $(xy)^n=x^ny^n$ are linearly independent. This is the invariant computation behind Brion Example 1.27(2), printed p. 10.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: The quotient of the plane by the hyperbolic multiplicative-group action
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. In the setting of [[lem-invariant-polynomials-of-the-hyperbolic-gm-action-on-the-plane]], let $G=\mathbf G_m$ act on $X=\mathbb C^2$ by $t\cdot(x,y)=(tx,t^{-1}y)$. Then: (i) the invariant ring is $\mathbb C[X]^G=\mathbb C[xy]$, so the categorical quotient is $\pi:X	o X/\!/G=\mathbb C$, $\pi(x,y)=xy$ ([[thm-invariant-ring-finite-generation-and-affine-categorical-quotient]]); (ii) the orbits are the hyperbolae $xy=c$ for $c
eq0$, the two punctured coordinate axes $\{x=0,y
eq0\}$, $\{y=0,x
eq0\}$, and the origin; the two punctured-axis orbits are not closed and their closures are the corresponding axes through the origin; the origin is closed and is the unique closed orbit in the fibre $\pi^{-1}(0)$; (iii) the stable locus is $X^s=\{xy
eq0\}$, $\pi(X^s)=\mathbb C^	imes$, and $\pi^s:X^s	o\mathbb C^	imes$ is a geometric quotient, a principal $\mathbf G_m$-bundle ([[thm-stable-locus-geometric-quotient]], [[def-stable-points-of-an-affine-action]]); the origin is unstable although its orbit is closed, its stabilizer being all of $\mathbf G_m$.
items.strategy: Part (i) uses the explicit invariant calculation and, once its source gate is closed, the affine quotient theorem. For (ii), if xy=c != 0, any two points of that fibre are carried to one another by the unique t=x'/x; the equation xy=c makes the fibre closed in the plane. On each punctured axis multiplication is transitive and its closure is the whole axis, since a polynomial vanishing at every nonzero complex number vanishes identically. The origin is fixed and closed. Thus the zero fibre has exactly these three orbits and only the origin is closed. Stabilizers are trivial at every nonzero point and are all of G_m at the origin. Consequently the closed orbits with finite stabilizers are exactly xy != 0. The map (x,y) -> (x,xy) identifies this open set with G_m x G_m, with inverse (t,c) -> (t,c/t), and the action is multiplication on the first factor. Projection onto c is thus a trivial principal G_m bundle and a geometric quotient. The affine quotient and stable-locus suppliers use the repaired local algebraic bridge; the explicit orbit and bundle computations also verify each specialized conclusion directly.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22
I. Dolgachev, Lectures on Invariant Theory (lecture notes, archived copy)

items.title: A closed orbit need not be stable: the trivial multiplicative-group action on a point
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. The assertion 'every point of a complex affine $G$-variety whose orbit is closed is stable' is false. Counterexample: $G=\mathbf G_m$ acts trivially on the one-point affine algebraic set $X=\{0\}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$; the unique orbit is closed, but the stabilizer $G_0=G$ is positive-dimensional, so the point is not stable ([[def-stable-points-of-an-affine-action]], [[def-reductive-and-linearly-reductive-over-c]]).
items.strategy: Brion Definition 1.25 requires both closedness of the orbit and finiteness of the stabilizer; the trivial action of $G=\mathbf G_m$ on a point has $G_0=G$ infinite. The example is the one prescribed by the AG-ACT-3 design (line 212) and is Brion Example 1.27(1) in its simplest form. It shows that the finite-stabilizer hypothesis of the stable-locus theorem cannot be dropped.

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22

items.title: The finite-group Noether theorem does not supply invariant finite generation for positive-dimensional groups
items.statement: Noether's finiteness theorem for invariants of a finite group ([[thm-noether-finiteness-theorem-for-invariants]]) requires the acting group to be finite. It therefore does not supply the finite generation of invariant rings of positive-dimensional groups: applied to the action of $\mathbf G_m=\mathbb C^\times$ on $\mathbb C^2$ of [[lem-invariant-polynomials-of-the-hyperbolic-gm-action-on-the-plane]] the hypothesis fails, since $\mathbf G_m$ is not finite, even though the invariant ring there is $\mathbb C[xy]$; and no argument on this page reduces a reductive group action to a finite-group action. The finite-group theorem is thus not a substitute for the Reynolds-operator proof of finite generation for complex reductive groups.
items.strategy: Hypothesis comparison only: the published theorem ([[thm-noether-finiteness-theorem-for-invariants]]) assumes a finite group; a positive-dimensional group such as $\mathbf G_m$ is not finite. The example of [[lem-invariant-polynomials-of-the-hyperbolic-gm-action-on-the-plane]] makes the failure of the hypothesis concrete without asserting any reduction. This records the caveat prescribed by the AG-ACT-3 design (line 212).

references.title: Michel Brion, Introduction to actions of algebraic groups, Les cours du CIRM 1 (2010), no. 1, 1-22
